8.t: Working with data: where substitutions fall
q: Calculate the percentage of all substitutions that are silent.
Explain why most silent substitutions are in the third base of the codon.
The genetic code is degenerate: many amino acids have several codons that differ only in the third base.
Explain why no substitution in the second base is silent.
Codons that share the same amino acid almost always share the first two bases, so a change in the second base always changes the amino acid (or makes a stop codon).
Suggest why nonsense mutations are the rarest kind in a population.
A stop codon produces a short, usually non-functional protein, which is often harmful, so these alleles are removed by natural selection.
A missense mutation may not affect the protein. Explain how.
The new amino acid may have similar properties, or be far from the active site, so the protein still folds and works.
Describe the relationship between the number of repeats and the age at onset.
More repeats, earlier onset (40 repeats: 62 years; 50 repeats: 28 years). The curve is steepest at lower repeat numbers.
State the type of mutation, and explain why the protein is longer.
An insertion (repeat expansion). CAG codes for glutamine, so the protein gets extra glutamines in a row.
A parent has 42 repeats and their child has 50. Predict the difference in age at onset, and suggest why the number grew.
About 52 against 28 years: about 24 years earlier. Repeats are unstable when DNA is copied during gamete formation, so the number can increase in the next generation.
Discuss whether a 16-year-old with an affected parent should be tested.
For: planning, reproductive choices, ending uncertainty. Against: no cure, heavy emotional burden, possible discrimination. Most clinics test only adults who choose it after counselling.

21.t: Working with data: cancer and age
q: Calculate how many times higher the rate is at 85 than at 45.
2200 / 180 = about 12 times.
Describe the trend.
The rate rises slowly to the 40s, then ever more steeply with age.
Explain the trend, using the idea that several mutations are needed.

Cancer usually needs several mutations (in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes) in one cell. Mutations accumulate over a lifetime, so the chance that one cell has them all rises steeply with age; repair and immune surveillance also decline.
Explain why rates are given per 100 000 people, not as numbers of cases.
Age groups contain different numbers of people, so rates allow a fair comparison.
Suggest two ways people can reduce their risk.
Any two: not smoking; sun protection; HPV vaccination; less alcohol; a healthy diet and weight.
